{{Short description|Method of finding chemicals in a database}}
{{Use British English|date=August 2024}}
[[File:Lenalidomide substructures.svg|thumb|The drug [[lenalidomide]] contains substructures [[isoindoline]] (red) and [[glutarimide]] (blue)]]
'''Substructure search''' ('''SSS''') is a method to retrieve from a [[Chemical database|database]] only those [[Chemical compound|chemicals]] matching a pattern of atoms and bonds which a user specifies. It is an application of [[graph theory]], specifically [[subgraph matching]] in which the query is a [[hydrogen-depleted molecular graph]]. The mathematical foundations for the method were laid in the 1870s, when it was suggested that [[Molecule editor|chemical structure drawing]]s were equivalent to graphs with atoms as vertices and bonds as edges. SSS is now a standard part of [[cheminformatics]] and is widely used by pharmaceutical chemists in [[drug discovery]].

There are many commercial systems that provide SSS, typically having a [[graphical user interface]] and chemical drawing software. Large publicly available databases like [[PubChem]] and [[ChemSpider]] can be searched this way, as can [[Wikipedia]]'s articles describing individual chemicals.

==Definitions==
Substructure search is used to retrieve from a [[chemical database|database of chemicals]] those which contain the pattern of atoms and bonds specified by a user. It is implemented using a specialist type of [[query language]] and in real-world applications the search may be further constrained using [[logical operator]]s on additional data held in the database. Thus "return all [[carboxylic acids]] where a sample of >1&nbsp;g is available".<ref name=Currano>{{cite book |doi=10.1039/9781782620655-00109  |chapter=Chapter 5. Searching by Structure and Substructure |title=Chemical Information for Chemists |date=2014 |last1=Currano |first1=Judith N. |pages=109–145 |isbn=978-1-84973-551-3 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1021/ci200413e |title=Efficient Substructure Searching of Large Chemical Libraries: The ABCD Chemical Cartridge |date=2011 |last1=Agrafiotis |first1=Dimitris K. |last2=Lobanov |first2=Victor S. |last3=Shemanarev |first3=Maxim |last4=Rassokhin |first4=Dmitrii N. |last5=Izrailev |first5=Sergei |last6=Jaeger |first6=Edward P. |last7=Alex |first7=Simson |last8=Farnum |first8=Michael |display-authors=3 |journal=Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling |volume=51 |issue=12 |pages=3113–3130 |pmid=22035187 }}</ref> One definition of "substructure" was provided in 2008: "given two chemical structures A and B, if structure A is fully contained in structure B, then A is a substructure of B, while B is a superstructure of A."<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1093/bioinformatics/btn186 |title=A maximum common substructure-based algorithm for searching and predicting drug-like compounds |date=2008 |last1=Cao |first1=Yiqun |last2=Jiang |first2=Tao |last3=Girke |first3=Thomas |journal=Bioinformatics |volume=24 |issue=13 |pages=i366–i374 |pmid=18586736 |pmc=2718661 }}</ref>
{{Quote box|width = 25% |title = [[International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry|IUPAC]] definition |quote = '''molecular graph''': The graph with differently labelled (coloured) vertices (chromatic graph) which represent different kinds of atoms and differently labelled (coloured) edges related to different types of bonds. Within the topological electron distribution theory, a complete network of the bond paths for a given nuclear configuration.<ref name=GoldBookMT07069>{{cite journal |title=molecular graph |journal=Gold Book |date=2014 |publisher=IUPAC |ref=Gold Book MT07069 |doi=10.1351/goldbook.MT07069 |doi-access=free }}</ref>}}
In this definition, the word "structure" is not synonymous with "[[Chemical compound|compound]]". If it were, the structure for [[ethanol]], {{chem2|CH3CH2OH}} would not be a substructure of [[propanol]], {{chem2|CH3CH2CH2OH}}, since the terminal CH<sub>3</sub> of ethanol is not ''fully contained'' at the propanol chain two atoms away from the OH group. Instead the query structure is, formally, a [[hydrogen-depleted molecular graph]]. The search is thus for substances which contain three atoms and two single bonds connected as C–C–O. Propanol is a "hit", as is [[diethyl ether]], with C–C–O–C–C. If a user wished to limit the hits to [[alcohols]], then the query structure would have to be drawn with an "explicit hydrogen", as C–C–O–H and ether would no longer match.<ref name=Currano/> In mathematical terms, finding substructures is an application of [[graph theory]], specifically [[subgraph matching]].<ref name=Ullmann>{{cite journal |doi=10.1145/321921.321925 |doi-access=free |title=An Algorithm for Subgraph Isomorphism |date=1976 |last1=Ullmann |first1=J. R. |journal=[[Journal of the ACM]] |volume=23 |pages=31–42 }}</ref>
===Examples===
Standard conventions used when chemists draw [[chemical structure]]s<ref name=McMurry>{{cite book |isbn=9781711471853 |title=Organic Chemistry: A Tenth Edition |last1=McMurry |first1=John |date=2023 |publisher=OpenStax, Rice University |url=https://openstax.org/details/books/organic-chemistry |chapter=1.12 Drawing Chemical Structures |pages=25–27 }}</ref> need to be considered when implementing substructure search. Historically, the representation of [[tautomer]]<ref name=Katritzky>{{cite journal |doi=10.1007/s10822-010-9359-z |title=Tautomerism in drug discovery |date=2010 |last1=Katritzky |first1=Alan R. |last2=Hall |first2=C. Dennis |last3=El-Gendy |first3=Bahaa El-Dien M. |last4=Draghici |first4=Bogdan |journal=Journal of Computer-Aided Molecular Design |volume=24 |issue=6–7 |pages=475–484 |pmid=20490619 |bibcode=2010JCAMD..24..475K }}</ref> forms and [[stereochemistry]]<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1093/toxsci/kfp097 |doi-access=free |title=Chiral Toxicology: It's the Same Thing…Only Different |date=2009 |last1=Smith |first1=Silas W. |journal=Toxicological Sciences |volume=110 |issue=1 |pages=4–30 |pmid=19414517 }}</ref> has posed difficulties. This can be illustrated using [[histidine]].<ref name=Warr2011>{{cite journal |doi=10.1002/wcms.36 |title=Representation of chemical structures |date=2011 |last1=Warr |first1=Wendy A. |journal=WIREs Computational Molecular Science |volume=1 |issue=4 |pages=557–579 }}</ref>
:[[File:Histidine isomers and tautomers.svg|upright=2]]
The top row shows the standard two-dimensional chemical drawing for (S)-histidine (the natural isomer of this [[amino acid]]), its [[enantiomer]] (R)-histidine and a drawing which conventionally indicates the [[racemic mixture]] of equal amounts of the R and S forms.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.chemspider.com/Search.aspx?q=histidine |title=Search term: histidine |website=chemspider.com |access-date=2024-08-01 }}</ref> The bottom row shows the same three compounds with the [[imidazole]] ring drawn in its alternative tautomer form. For histidine, it has been experimentally determined by <sup>15</sup>N NMR spectroscopy that the 1-H tautomer is preferred over the 3-H form in samples.<ref>{{cite book|title=ABCs of FT-NMR|last=Roberts|first=John D.|publisher=University Science Books|year=2000|isbn=978-1-891389-18-4|location=Sausalito, CA|pages=258–9}}</ref> Choice of representation for storage in a database can influence substucture searches. All six drawings are hits for a propanol substructure C–C–C–O, as shown in red. However, only the top row would, apparently, be a hit for the blue substructure of 1-H imidazole-4-methyl, as this is not ''fully contained'' in the other three compounds. In fact, each vertical pair is the same chemical substance: tautomers in general cannot be isolated as separate samples.<ref name=Katritzky/> In modern databases, substances are held in a single [[canonical form]], with checks made for uniqueness. The [[International Chemical Identifier#InChIKey|InChIKey]] provides one way to do this.<ref name=Warr2011/> (S)-Histidine's standard key is HNDVDQJCIGZPNO-YFKPBYRVSA-N,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.chemspider.com/Chemical-Structure.6038.html |title=L-Histidine |at=More details |website=chemspider.com |access-date=2024-08-01 }}</ref> (R)-histidine's key is HNDVDQJCIGZPNO-RXMQYKEDSA-N<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.chemspider.com/Chemical-Structure.64237.html |title=D-Histidine |at=More details |website=chemspider.com |access-date=2024-08-01 }}</ref> and (RS)-histidine's is HNDVDQJCIGZPNO-UHFFFAOYSA-N.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.chemspider.com/Chemical-Structure.752.html |title=DL-Histidine |at=More details |website=chemspider.com |access-date=2024-08-01 }}</ref> The first block of 14 letters is identical for all these substances, as it encodes the molecular graph.<ref name=Warr2011/>

==Query interfaces and search algorithms==
Most substructure search systems present the user with a [[graphical user interface]] with a [[Molecule editor|chemical structure drawing]] component. Query structures may contain bonding patterns such as "single/aromatic" or "any" to provide flexibility. Similarly, the vertices which in an actual compound would be a specific atom may be replaced with an atom list in the query. [[Cis–trans isomerism|''Cis''–''trans'' isomerism]] at [[double bond]]s is catered for by giving a choice of retrieving only the [[E–Z notation|E form]], the [[E–Z notation|Z form]], or both.<ref name=Currano/><ref name=Pubchem>{{cite web |url=https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/search/help_search.html |title=PubChem Structure Search |website=pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov |access-date=2024-08-01}}</ref>

The algorithms for searching are computationally intensive, often of [[Big O notation|O]]&nbsp;(''n''<sup>3</sup>) or O&nbsp;(''n''<sup>4</sup>) time complexity (where ''n'' is the number of atoms involved) but the problem is known to be [[NP-complete]].<ref>{{cite book |title=Complexity Theory: Exploring the Limits of Efficient Algorithms |first=Ingo |last=Wegener |publisher=Springer |year=2005 |isbn=9783540210450 |page=81 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1fo7_KoFUPsC&pg=PA81}}</ref> Speedups are achieved using fragment screening as a first step. This pre-computation typically involves creation of [[bitstring]]s representing presence or absence of molecular fragments. Target compounds that do not possess the fragments present in the query cannot be hits and are eliminated.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1021/ci60020a012 |title=On-Line Storage and Retrieval of Chemical Information. II. Substructure and Biological Activity Searching |date=1979 |last1=Bond |first1=V. Lynn |last2=Bowman |first2=Carlos M. |last3=Davison |first3=Linda C. |last4=Roush |first4=Patricia F. |last5=McGrew |first5=Roger D. |last6=Williams |first6=Daniel G. |display-authors=3 |journal=Journal of Chemical Information and Computer Sciences |volume=19 |issue=4 |pages=231–234 |pmid=551973 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Cummings |first1= Maxwell D.|last2= Maxwell|first2= Alan C.|last3= DesJarlais|first3= Renee L. |year=2007| title= Processing of Small Molecule Databases for Automated Docking|journal= Medicinal Chemistry |volume=3|issue=1|pages=107–113|doi=10.2174/157340607779317481|pmid= 17266630}}</ref> Atom-by-atom-searching, in which a mapping of the query's atoms and bonds with the target molecule is sought, is usually done with a variant of the Ullman algorithm.<ref name=Ullmann/><ref name="SMSD09">{{cite journal |first1=S. A. |last1=Rahman |first2= M. |last2=Bashton |first3= G. L. |last3= Holliday |first4= R. |last4=Schrader |first5=J. M. |last5=Thornton |year=2000 |title=Small Molecule Subgraph Detector (SMSD) toolkit|journal= Journal of Cheminformatics |volume=1 |issue=1 |page=12 |doi=10.1186/1758-2946-1-12 |doi-access=free |pmid=20298518 |pmc=2820491  }}</ref>

==Implementations==
{{As of|2024}}, substructure search is a standard feature in [[List of chemical databases|chemical databases accessible via the web]]. Large databases such as [[PubChem]],<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1002/cpz1.217 |title=Exploring Chemical Information in PubChem |date=2021 |last1=Kim |first1=Sunghwan |journal=Current Protocols |volume=1 |issue=8 |pages=e217 |pmid=34370395 |pmc=8363119 }}</ref><ref name=Pubchem/> maintained by the [[National Center for Biotechnology Information]] and [[ChemSpider]],<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1021/bk-2010-1060.ch002 |chapter=ChemSpider: Integrating Structure-Based Resources Distributed across the Internet |title=Enhancing Learning with Online Resources, Social Networking, and Digital Libraries |series=ACS Symposium Series |date=2010 |last1=Williams |first1=Antony J. |volume=1060 |pages=23–39 |isbn=978-0-8412-2600-5 }}</ref> maintained by the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] have graphical interfaces for search. The [[Chemical Abstracts Service]], a division of the [[American Chemical Society]],  provides tools to search the chemical literature and [[Reaxys]] supplied by [[Elsevier]] covers both chemicals and reaction information, including that originally held in the [[Beilstein database]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1021/acs.jchemed.9b00966 |title=Property Information in Substance Records in Major Web-Based Chemical Information and Data Retrieval Tools: Understanding Content, Search Opportunities, and Application to Teaching |date=2020 |last1=Jarabak |first1=Charlotte |last2=Mutton |first2=Troy |last3=Ridley |first3=Damon D. |journal=Journal of Chemical Education |volume=97 |issue=5 |pages=1345–1359 |bibcode=2020JChEd..97.1345J }}</ref> [[Patentscope|PATENTSCOPE]] maintained by the [[World Intellectual Property Organization]] makes chemical patents accessible by substructure<ref>{{Cite web |title=Substructure Search Now Available in PATENTSCOPE |url=https://www.wipo.int/patentscope/en/news/pctdb/2019/news_0001.html |date=2019-02-11 |access-date=2024-08-04 |website=www.wipo.int }}</ref> and Wikipedia's articles describing individual chemicals can also be searched that way.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1186/s13321-015-0061-y |doi-access=free |title=Wikipedia Chemical Structure Explorer: Substructure and similarity searching of molecules from Wikipedia |date=2015 |last1=Ertl |first1=Peter |last2=Patiny |first2=Luc |last3=Sander |first3=Thomas |last4=Rufener |first4=Christian |last5=Zasso |first5=Michaël |display-authors=3 |journal=Journal of Cheminformatics |volume=7 |page=10 |pmid=25815062 |pmc=4374119 }}</ref>

Suppliers of chemicals as synthesis intermediates or for [[high-throughput screening]] routinely provide search interfaces. Currently, the largest database that can be freely searched by the public is the [[ZINC database]], which is claimed to contain over 37 billion commercially available molecules.<ref name=ZINC>{{cite journal |doi=10.1021/acs.jcim.2c01253 |doi-access=free |title=ZINC-22─A Free Multi-Billion-Scale Database of Tangible Compounds for Ligand Discovery |date=2023 |last1=Tingle |first1=Benjamin I. |last2=Tang |first2=Khanh G. |last3=Castanon |first3=Mar |last4=Gutierrez |first4=John J. |last5=Khurelbaatar |first5=Munkhzul |last6=Dandarchuluun |first6=Chinzorig |last7=Moroz |first7=Yurii S. |last8=Irwin |first8=John J. |journal=Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling |volume=63 |issue=4 |pages=1166–1176 |pmid=36790087 |pmc=9976280 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1021/acs.jcim.2c00224 |title=Exploration of Ultralarge Compound Collections for Drug Discovery |date=2022 |last1=Warr |first1=Wendy A. |last2=Nicklaus |first2=Marc C. |last3=Nicolaou |first3=Christos A. |last4=Rarey |first4=Matthias |journal=Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling |volume=62 |issue=9 |pages=2021–2034 |pmid=35421301 }}</ref>

==History==
{{Further|Chemical graph generator}}
[[File:Historic Benzene Formulae Kekulé (original).png|thumb|Kekulé structure of benzene, 1872 ]]
The idea that chemical structures as depicted using drawings of the type introduced by [[August Kekulé|Kekulé]] were related to what is now called [[graph theory]] was suggested by the mathematician [[James Joseph Sylvester|J. J. Sylvester]] in 1878. He was the first to use the word "graph" in the sense of a [[Network theory|network]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/017284a0 |doi-access=free |title=Chemistry and Algebra |date=1878 |last1=Sylvester |first1=J. J. |journal=Nature |volume=17 |issue=432 |page=284 |bibcode=1878Natur..17..284S |quote=Every invariant and covariant thus becomes expressible by a ''graph'' precisely identical with a Kekuléan diagram or chemicograph.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |title= Handbook of graph theory |first1=Jonathan L. |last1=Gross |first2=Jay |last2=Yellen |publisher=[[CRC Press]] |year=2004 |page=35 |isbn=978-1-58488-090-5 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mKkIGIea_BkC&pg=PA35 |access-date=2024-07-28 }}</ref> [[Arthur Cayley]] had already, in 1874, considered how to enumerate chemical [[isomers]], in what was an early approach to [[molecular graph]]s, where atoms are at [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] and bonds correspond to [[Glossary_of_graph_theory#edge|edges]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1080/14786447408641058 |title=LVII. ''On the mathematical theory of isomers'' |date=1874 |last1=Cayley |journal=The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science |volume=47 |issue=314 |pages=444–447 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |isbn=0198539169 |title=[[Graph Theory, 1736-1936]] |last1=Biggs |first1=Norman |author-link=Norman L. Biggs |last2=Keith Lloyd |first2=E. |last3=Wilson |first3=Robin J. |author-link3=Robin Wilson (mathematician) |date=1986 |pages=39, 63–64 |publisher=Clarendon Press }}</ref>
{{Quote box|width = 25% |title = [[International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry|IUPAC]] definition |quote = '''structural formula''': A formula which gives information about the way the atoms in a molecule are connected and arranged in space.<ref name=GoldBookS06061>{{cite journal |title=structural formula |journal=Gold Book |date=2014 |publisher=IUPAC |ref=Gold Book S06061 |doi=10.1351/goldbook.S06061|doi-access=free }}</ref>}}
In the 20th century, chemists developed standard ways to show [[structural formula]], especially for individual [[organic compounds]] that were increasingly being synthesized and tested as potential drugs or agrochemicals,<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1007/s10698-007-9033-2 |title=Structural formulas and explanation in organic chemistry |date=2008 |last1=Goodwin |first1=W. M. |journal=Foundations of Chemistry |volume=10 |issue=2 |pages=117–127 }}</ref><ref name=McMurry/> By the 1950s, as the number of compounds made and tested grew, the first attempts to create [[chemical databases]] were made and the sub-discipline of [[cheminformatics]] was established.<ref name=Willett>{{cite journal |doi=10.1177/0165551507084631  |title=From chemical documentation to chemoinformatics: 50 years of chemical information science |date=2008 |last1=Willett |first1=Peter |journal=Journal of Information Science |volume=34 |issue=4 |pages=477–499 }}</ref> As stated in 2012, "searching for substructures in molecules belongs to the most elementary tasks in cheminformatics and is nowadays part of virtually every cheminformatics software".<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1186/1758-2946-4-13 |doi-access=free |title=Systematic benchmark of substructure search in molecular graphs - from Ullmann to VF2 |date=2012 |last1=Ehrlich |first1=Hans-Christian |last2=Rarey |first2=Matthias |journal=Journal of Cheminformatics |volume=4 |issue=1 |page=13 |pmid=22849361 |pmc=3586954 }}</ref>
[[File:Markush structure.svg|left|thumb|Example of a [[Markush structure]]]]
The first suggested use for substructure search was in 1957, to reduce the workload of [[patent examiners]]. They have to search published literature to decide whether an invention is novel, which for [[chemical patents]] often means finding known examples within the generic claims of a Markush structure.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1126/science.126.3278.814  |title=Finding Chemical Records by Digital Computers |date=1957 |last1=Ray |first1=Louis C. |last2=Kirsch |first2=Russell A. |journal=Science |volume=126 |issue=3278 |pages=814–819 |pmid=17776535 |bibcode=1957Sci...126..814R }}</ref><ref name=Willett/> Before this could become a reality, a number of developments were required. Importantly, the existing literature had to be made searchable and a way to input a [[Molecule editor|chemical structure query]] and return the matching results had to devised. These requirements had been partially met as early as 1881 when [[Friedrich Konrad Beilstein]] introduced the ''[[Beilstein database|Handbuch der organischen Chemie]]'' (''Handbook of Organic Chemistry'') which carefully classified known chemicals in a very systematic manner so that all examples containing a given [[heterocycle]] would be located together.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1021/ed015p310 |title=How Beilstein is made |date=1938 |last1=Richter |first1=Friedrich |journal=Journal of Chemical Education |volume=15 |issue=7 |page=310 |bibcode=1938JChEd..15..310R }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1039/9781782620655-00053  |chapter=Chapter 3. Chemical Patents |title=Chemical Information for Chemists |date=2014 |last1=White |first1=Michael J. |pages=53–90 |isbn=978-1-84973-551-3 }}</ref>

In 1907, the [[American Chemical  Society]] set up the [[Chemical Abstracts Service]] (CAS). This weekly subscription service included a printed publication with summaries of articles in thousands of scholarly journals and claims in worldwide patents. This had a chemical substance index that, in principle, allowed searching by chemical name or formula.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cas.org/products/print/index.html |title=CAS Printed Products |publisher=CAS |access-date=2024-07-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080512161918/http://www.cas.org/products/print/ca/index.html |archive-date=2008-05-12 |url-status=dead }}</ref> However, it was only when the CAS records had been fully converted into [[machine-readable]] form and the internet was available to connect its database to end-users that comprehensive searching became possible. CAS provided various specialist search services from the 1980s but it was not until 2008 that its "SciFinder" system became available via [[the web]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cas.org/newsevents/releases/scifinderweb040708.html |title=New SciFinder Available Via the Web |publisher=CAS |access-date=2024-07-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080513152556/http://www.cas.org/newsevents/releases/scifinderweb040708.html |archive-date=2008-05-13 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

By the 1960s, companies synthesizing and testing new chemicals made significant progress in creating in-house databases. [[Imperial Chemical Industries]] stored chemical structures encoded as text [[string (computer science)|strings]], using [[Wiswesser line notation]]. Its associated CROSSBOW software allowed substructure search using key-based searches followed by more processor-intensive atom-by-atom search.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1002/ps.2780050316 |title=The use of computers with chemical structural information: ICI CROSSBOW system |date=1974 |last1=Eakin |first1=Diane R. |last2=Hyde |first2=Ernest |last3=Palmer |first3=Graham |journal=Pesticide Science |volume=5 |issue=3 |pages=319–326 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1021/ci00034a007  |title=Diverse uses and future prospects for Wiswesser line-formula notation |date=1982 |last1=Warr |first1=Wendy A. |journal=Journal of Chemical Information and Computer Sciences |volume=22 |issue=2 |pages=98–101 }}</ref> It was recognised that research chemists wanted not only to search company collections for existing inventory but also to search third-party databases supplied by vendors of small-molecule intermediates. The latter application evolved as a collaboration involving six companies with pharmaceutical interests and their commercial suppliers.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1021/ci00037a001 |title=Development of CAOCI and its use in ICI plant protection division |date=1983 |last1=Walker |first1=S. Barrie |journal=Journal of Chemical Information and Computer Sciences |volume=23 |pages=3–5 }}</ref><ref name=Warr2011/>

By the 1980s, other line notations were used for commercially available substructure search systems. [[SMILES]] encoding, together with its [[SMILES arbitrary target specification|SMARTS]] query language,<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1021/ci00057a005 |title=SMILES, a chemical language and information system. 1. Introduction to methodology and encoding rules |date=1988 |last1=Weininger |first1=David |journal=Journal of Chemical Information and Computer Sciences |volume=28 |pages=31–36 }}</ref> and [[SYBYL line notation]]<ref name=Warr2011/><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1021/ci7004687 |title=SYBYL Line Notation (SLN): A Single Notation to Represent Chemical Structures, Queries, Reactions, and Virtual Libraries |date=2008 |last1=Homer |first1=R. Webster |last2=Swanson |first2=Jon |last3=Jilek |first3=Robert J. |last4=Hurst |first4=Tad |last5=Clark |first5=Robert D. |display-authors=3 |journal=Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling |volume=48 |issue=12 |pages=2294–2307 |pmid=18998666 }}</ref> are examples.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1021/ci00047a023 |title=Historic development of chemical notations |date=1985 |last1=Wiswesser |first1=William J. |journal=Journal of Chemical Information and Computer Sciences |volume=25 |issue=3 |pages=258–263 }}</ref> A comprehensive survey of then-available chemical information systems was produced for [[NASA]] in 1985.<ref name=NASA>{{cite web |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19890005600/downloads/19890005600.pdf |date=1985-12-05 |last=Shaik |first=Aneesa Bashir |title=A survey of chemical information systems |pages=1–160 |website=ntrs.nasa.gov }}</ref>

The need to combine chemistry search with biological data produced by screening compounds at ever-larger scales led to implementation of systems such as MACCS.<ref name=NASA/>{{rp|73–77}}<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1021/ci00046a007  |title=Use of MACCS within ICI |date=1985 |last1=Adamson |first1=George W. |last2=Bird |first2=John M. |last3=Palmer |first3=Graham |last4=Warr |first4=Wendy A. |journal=Journal of Chemical Information and Computer Sciences |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=90–92 }}</ref> This commercial system from [[MDL Information Systems]] made use of an algorithm specifically designed for storage and search within groups of chemicals that differed only in their stereochemistry.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1021/ja00822a021 |title=Stereochemically unique naming algorithm |date=1974 |last1=Wipke |first1=W. Todd |last2=Dyott |first2=Thomas M. |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |volume=96 |issue=15 |pages=4834–4842 |bibcode=1974JAChS..96.4834W }}</ref> A review of the many systems available by the mid-1980s pointed out that "most in-house developed systems have been replaced with commercially available standardised software for managing chemical structure databases."<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-73975-0_3  |chapter=Current Approaches and New Directions in the Management of In-House Chemical Structure Databases |title=Chemical Structures |date=1988 |last1=Hagadone |first1=Tom R. |pages=23–41 |isbn=978-3-642-73977-4 }}</ref> The [[MDL Molfile]] is now an [[open file format]] for storing single-molecule data in the form of a connection table.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://discover.3ds.com/sites/default/files/2020-08/biovia_ctfileformats_2020.pdf |title=CT File Formats |author=<!--Not stated-->  |publisher=Biovia |date=August 2020 |access-date=2024-08-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210219065450/https://discover.3ds.com/sites/default/files/2020-08/biovia_ctfileformats_2020.pdf |archive-date=2021-02-19 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=Warr2011/>

By the 2000s, [[personal computers]] had become powerful enough that storage and search of chemistry within [[office software]] such as [[Microsoft Excel]] was possible.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1186/1758-2946-4-3 |doi-access=free |title=LICSS - a chemical spreadsheet in microsoft excel |date=2012 |last1=Lawson |first1=Kevin R. |last2=Lawson |first2=Jonty |journal=Journal of Cheminformatics |volume=4 |issue=1 |page=3 |pmid=22301088 |pmc=3310842 }}</ref>

Subsequent developments involved the use of new techniques to allow efficient searches over very large databases and, importantly, the use of a standardised [[International Chemical Identifier]], a type of line notation, to uniquely define a chemical substance.<ref name=Warr2011/><ref name=ZINC/><ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1039/9781788016186-00084 |last=Judson |first=Philip |chapter=Chapter 7. Structure, Substructure and Superstructure Searching |title=Knowledge-based Expert Systems in Chemistry |series=Theoretical and Computational Chemistry Series |date=2019 |pages=84–107 |publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry |isbn=978-1-78801-471-7 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1021/acs.jcim.2c00390 |doi-access=free |title=Special Issue on Reaction Informatics and Chemical Space |date=2022 |last1=Rarey |first1=Matthias |last2=Nicklaus |first2=Marc C. |last3=Warr |first3=Wendy |journal=Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling |volume=62 |issue=9 |pages=2009–2010 |pmid=35527682 }}</ref>
